questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates your ability to design a secure, scalable architecture for exposing private backend services to external partners while maintaining strict security controls and backend privacy.

## Architecture Overview

```
External Partners
       │
       ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│ Azure Front Door │ ◄── DDoS Protection Standard + WAF + IP Allowlist
└────────┬────────┘
         │
         ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Azure API Management     │ ◄── JWT Validation + Rate Limiting
│ (Regional Self-Hosted GW)│
└────────┬─────────────────┘
         │ (Private Link)
         ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Private Backend API      │ ◄── AKS/VM in Private Subnet
│ (No Public Exposure)     │
└─────────────────────────┘
```

## Key Components

| Service | Purpose |
|---------|--------|
| Azure Front Door | Global routing, DDoS Protection Standard, WAF, CDN |
| Azure API Management | Gateway with JWT validation, rate limiting, policy engine |
| Azure Private Link | Secure private connectivity to backend |
| Azure AD | OAuth 2.0 / OIDC token issuance and validation |

## IP Allowlisting Configuration

### Option 1: Front Door WAF IP Restriction (Recommended)
```json
{
  "name": "IpAllowlistRule",
  "priority": 100,
  "enabled": true,
  "ruleType": "MatchRule",
  "matchConditions": [
    {
      "matchVariable": "RemoteAddr",
      "operator": "IPMatch",
      "negate": true,
      "matchValue": [
        "203.0.113.0/24",
        "198.51.100.0/24"
      ]
    }
  ],
  "action": "Block",
  "matchProcessingBehavior": "Stop"
}
```

### Option 2: APIM IP Filter Policy
```xml
<policies>
  <inbound>
    <ip-filter action="allow">
      <address>203.0.113.0</address>
      <address>198.51.100.0</address>
      <subnet>255.255.255.0</subnet>
    </ip-filter>
    <base />
  </inbound>
</policies>
```

## JWT Validation with Azure AD (APIM Policy)
```xml
<policies>
  <inbound>
    <validate-jwt header-name="Authorization" failed-validation-httpcode="401" failed-validation-error-message="Unauthorized. Invalid or expired token.">
      <issuer-signing-keys>
        <key jwk-id="https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenantId}/discovery/v2.0/keys" resolver="https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenantId}/.well-known/openid-configuration" />
      </issuer-signing-keys>
      <audiences>
        <audience>api://{apiClientId}</audience>
      </audiences>
      <issuers>
        <issuer>https://sts.windows.net/{tenantId}/</issuer>
      </issuers>
      <required-claims>
        <claim name="aud">
          <value>api://{apiClientId}</value>
        </claim>
      </required-claims>
    </validate-jwt>
    <base />
  </inbound>
</policies>
```

## Per-Client Rate Limiting
```xml
<policies>
  <inbound>
    <rate-limit-by-key calls="100" renewal-period="60" counter-key="context.Request.IpAddress" />
    <quota-by-key calls="1000" renewal-period="3600" counter-key="context.Subscription.Id" />
    <base />
  </inbound>
</policies>
```

## Azure AD App Registration Configuration
1. Register application in Azure AD with:
   - Expose an API (Application ID URI)
   - Add client scopes for partner access
   - Configure partner application permissions
2. Partners obtain tokens via:
   - Client credentials flow (service-to-service)
   - Authorization code flow (user delegation)
3. APIM validates tokens against Azure AD JWKS endpoint

## Critical Design Considerations

- **Private Link ensures backend never has public IP** - Backend pods/VMs have no public endpoints
- **Defense-in-depth with dual IP filtering** - Block at both WAF and APIM layers
- **Token validation at gateway** - Reject unauthorized requests before they reach backend
- **Rate limiting per client-id** - Prevents individual clients from consuming excessive resources
- **Managed identity for Private Link** - APIM uses system-managed identity to connect to backend privately

## Common Mistakes to Avoid
- Exposing backend directly via Application Gateway without proper network isolation
- Implementing rate limiting at application layer instead of gateway layer
- Hardcoding IP allowlists instead of using Azure-managed WAF rules
- Skipping Private Link and relying on NSG-based security alone

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests the ability to design a compliant, multi-tenant analytics stack using core Azure fundamentals, balancing isolation, governance, cost optimization, and disaster recovery.

## Key Concepts

- **Data Lake Gen2** landing and zone design (bronze/silver/gold layers)
- **Event-driven processing** with Event Grid and Azure Functions
- **Tenant isolation** via Entra ID RBAC, managed identities, and role-based access controls
- **Data cataloging and lineage** with Azure Purview
- **IaC + CI/CD** with GitHub Actions and Terraform
- **Cost governance** through resource tagging, budgets, and right-sizing
- **Cross-region DR** using geo-redundant storage and read replicas

## Architecture Overview

1. **Ingest**: Telemetry lands in Data Lake Gen2 (bronze layer)
2. **Process**: Event Grid triggers Functions to transform data (silver/gold layers)
3. **Serve**: Curated metrics published to Synapse Serverless SQL with per-tenant views
4. **Secure**: Entra ID RBAC + managed identities enforce tenant isolation
5. **Catalog**: Purview provides data discovery and lineage tracking
6. **Automate**: GitHub Actions + Terraform manage infrastructure lifecycle
7. **Govern**: Cost alerts and budgets ensure financial accountability

## Why This Is Asked
This scenario tests practical Azure fundamentals: streaming ingestion, cross-region disaster recovery, private networking, identity management, cost governance, and CI/CD for infrastructure-as-code. It also evaluates the ability to balance latency requirements with regional locality and budget constraints.

- **Event Hubs Standard** with auto-inflate for elastic throughput

- **Synapse DW** with private endpoints for secure data warehousing
- **Entra ID** and RBAC for identity-driven access control
- **Azure Private Link** for private endpoint connectivity
- **RA-GRS** storage with geo-DR alias for disaster recovery
- Cost governance through budgets and right-sizing
- GitHub Actions for IaC validation and deployment

## Architecture Overview
The mobile-game telemetry pipeline sends events to Event Hubs in Region A. A Databricks job continuously reads, aggregates on an hourly basis, and writes to Synapse DW. Private endpoints ensure all network traffic stays within the virtual network. For DR, enable RA-GRS on the storage account and use a geo-DR alias to fail over to Region B if Region A becomes unavailable.

## Cost-Conscious Considerations
- Use Event Hubs auto-inflate to scale throughput only when needed
- Choose appropriate Synapse DW performance tier for workload
- Implement budgets and alerts to monitor spending
- Leverage Reserved Instances for predictable workloads


```javascript
az network private-dns zone create -g rg -n privatelink.blob.core.windows.net
```
